source.title: Which Minimizer Does My Neural Network Converge To?
source.authors: Manuel Nonnenmacher; David Reeb; Ingo Steinwart

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: Experiments compare test performance across optimizers and batch sizes, while the analysis studies how those training choices change the converged minimizer.
record.gate_note: The text also cites earlier optimizer and initialization results; those are not recorded as this study’s results. The plotted curves do not provide recoverable numeric values in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares held-out loss after GD, AdaGrad and Adam training to similarly low training loss, bearing on V4. Its batch-size experiments train to a loss threshold rather than a fixed epoch budget, so they do not test V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors explain how initialization and adaptive optimization change the converged predictor and test performance. Mini-batch size adds a path-dependent effect for adaptive methods, whereas ordinary SGD and GD yield essentially the same predictor under their assumptions. They report worse test error for adaptive methods in their experiments and propose reducing initialization scale to mitigate initialization-induced error.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses squared-loss, overparameterized ReLU networks and compares GD, AdaGrad, Adam, and batch-size conditions; it does not reproduce the broader benchmark recipes described in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Test performance varies with optimizer, initialization scale, and, for adaptive optimization, mini-batch size. Non-adaptive SGD shows weak batch-size and ordering dependence.

fits_no_version.finding: After training to low loss, AdaGrad test performance depends noticeably on batch size and ordering, whereas vanilla SGD largely matches full-batch GD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In strongly overparameterized networks trained to convergence under squared loss, batch size can change adaptive optimizers' final predictors and held-out loss, while ordinary SGD and GD yield nearly the same predictor.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger initialization scale can substantially increase held-out loss despite similarly low training loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization scale can affect the converged predictor and generalization of overparameterized networks.

record.problems: The optimizer and batch-size figures provide plotted results without numeric values in the supplied text. Experiments use 100 training samples for the primary MNIST and Fashion-MNIST settings and 100 test points; the text notes that some theoretical conditions do not hold for modern architectures or cross-entropy loss.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure 3 and Figure 4 do not state separate numeric values in the text, so results are recorded only at the aggregate level explicitly described by the authors.

untested.parts: No comparison of natural-label and random-label fitting and held-out performance.
No identified interpolation threshold or explicit result establishing continued test-error reduction beyond it.
No controlled convolutional versus fully connected comparison or local-connectivity intervention.

Language benchmarks, broader hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay and switching optimizers are not tested. The main comparisons use full-batch GD and adaptive methods with convergence-based stopping.
No fixed-epoch comparison of large and small batches, or controlled evaluation of recipe adaptations that remove a fixed-budget penalty.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurements or ranking of generalization measures.
No removal of memorized examples and retraining.

missing.what: Fashion-MNIST optimizer comparison replicating the Figure 3 performance pattern. Add a separate dataset row; Appendix E explicitly describes the results as almost identical.
Optimizer comparisons across training-set sizes and initialization scales, including less strongly overparameterized networks. These conditions are absent from R1 and are not declared omitted.

Optimizer comparisons extending to ResNet-20 on binary CIFAR-10 under squared loss and fully connected MNIST networks under cross-entropy loss. Record separately by optimizer, initialization and training-set size; the supplied figure text does not establish each comparison's direction.
missing.locator: Figure 5 and its caption; Sections 7 and 9

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V4. Remove both proposed V5 verdicts: convergence-based batch-size comparisons neither support nor challenge the fixed-epoch claim. Figure text supplies no reliable method-by-width numerical values; none are reconstructed.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or held-out chance comparison.
Widths vary, but the study does not test widening past the width needed for zero training error as a generalization claim.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.
Adaptive optimizer comparisons are reported in Figure 3, but separate numeric results for optimizer and width are figure-only; the text provides only an aggregate statement.
The batch-size comparison is for the tested network and optimizer settings, not broad image-classification and language benchmarks or fixed epoch budgets.

rows.subject: NNs with L = 2 and L = 3 layers; widths varied
rows.stage_stated: Trained to the same low empirical error.
rows.operation_detail: Train with vanilla GD, AdaGrad, or Adam; compare test error.
rows.baseline: Vanilla GD; exact values not stated in text.
rows.value: The authors report a significant performance gap between vanilla GD and the adaptive methods; exact values not stated in text.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 3 reports test error bars, but their values are not stated in text.
rows.note: Aggregate textual result across the tested widths and adaptive methods; Figure 3 does not support recovering separate method-by-width values from the supplied text.
rows.check: The reported gap favors GD: Section 9 explicitly states that adaptive methods have worse test error. Specify that the measure is held-out squared loss, not classification error rate. Training stops when empirical loss first falls below 1e-5; adaptive learning rates are chosen for monotonic training-loss decay.

rows.subject: NNs with L = 2 layers; widths m = 1000 and m = 4000
rows.stage_stated: Trained to a very low training error.
rows.operation_detail: Train with adaptive mini-batch SGD (AdaGrad) at varied batch-size split ratios; compare test error.

conditions.value: Varied by split ratio of training set size

rows.measure: Test error dependence on batch size and data ordering.
rows.baseline: Vanilla GD corresponds to split = 1.0; exact values not stated in text.
rows.value: The authors state that test performance becomes dependent on batch size; exact values not stated in text.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 4 reports error bars, but their values are not stated in text.
rows.note: The text describes the adaptive-optimization effect as noticeable. Specific split-by-width values are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: Batch-size dependence alone does not establish a large-batch penalty, and epochs are not held fixed. All models train until empirical loss falls below 1e-5. Also, split = 1.0 here denotes full-batch AdaGrad, not vanilla GD.

rows.subject: NNs with L = 2 layers; widths m = 1000 and m = 4000
rows.stage_stated: Trained to a very low training error.
rows.operation_detail: Train with non-adaptive SGD at varied batch-size split ratios; compare test error.

conditions.value: Varied by split ratio of training set size

rows.measure: Test error dependence on batch size and data ordering.
rows.baseline: Vanilla GD at split = 1.0; exact values not stated in text.
rows.value: The authors describe only weak dependency on batch size and ordering, and say SGD-trained networks have basically the same test error as GD at split = 1.0.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 4 reports error bars, but their values are not stated in text.
rows.note: This control qualifies the batch-size effect: it is weak for non-adaptive SGD and noticeable for adaptive optimization.
rows.check: The text describes essentially absent batch-size dependence after convergence, rather than a partial fixed-budget large-batch penalty. This experiment cannot determine V5 because training duration varies to reach the loss threshold.

relationships.condition: Overparameterized fully connected ReLU networks on MNIST 0 versus 1, with one or two hidden layers, trained under squared loss with limited learning-rate selection.
relationships.reason: R1 reports worse held-out loss for AdaGrad and Adam than GD despite similarly low training loss; Section 9 explicitly establishes the direction.
relationships.display_finding: The reported higher held-out losses for AdaGrad and Adam than GD despite similarly low training losses remain unverified.

relationships.condition: Fashion-MNIST 0 versus 1 in the Figure 8 optimizer comparison.
relationships.reason: Based on text missing from the rows: Appendix E and Figure 8 describe the same optimizer-performance pattern as Figure 3, with larger test losses.
relationships.display_finding: The reported recurrence of the optimizer-performance pattern with larger test losses remains unverified.
